newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Inter-ethnic parliament meets for first time.
newsitem.headline: Inter-ethnic parliament meets for first time.

text.p: Bosnian Moslem, Croat and Serb politicians convened the first full session of the country's peacetime parliament on Friday, ending three months of disputes over venues and other symbolic issues.
The 42-member House of Representatives, elected in post-war polls in September, met in Sarajevo's city centre at the national museum and a former front line.

The parliament was to approve cabinet nominations submitted by the three-man collective presidency, comprising Moslem chairman Alija Izetbegovic, Serb member Momcilo Krajisnik and Croat representative Kresimir Zubak.
Serb deputies boycotted a would-be inaugural session of parliament in the Bosnian capital in October, snubbing foreign dignitaries who had flown in for the ceremony.
The nationalist Serbs had cited objections to the venue in the city centre and to the text of an oath pledging loyalty to Bosnia as a single state.
Since then the senior Serb parliament member has signed the "solemn declaration" and international mediators said the other Serb deputies were expected to follow suit.
A 15-member upper chamber, the House of Peoples, was also to convene on Friday for the first time -- in the Sarajevo suburb of Lukavica in Serb-controlled territory.

Serb nationalist leaders have succeeded in persuading their Moslem and Croat rivals to accept rotating the venue for government meetings between the country's Serb republic and Moslem-Croat federation.
Just getting the parliament to meet at all is considered an achievement by Western diplomats anxious to see the new government begin functioning.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and Supreme Allied Commander General George Joulwan were due to visit the Bosnian capital on Friday to mark the formation of the peacetime government.
A NATO-led peace force of 35,000 troops is currently deployed in Bosnia to police a U.S.-brokered peace treaty signed a year ago.

If all goes as planned, the parliament will approve the cabinet known as the Council of Ministers. The council is a weak central government ruling Bosnia's autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat territories.

A Moslem and a Serb serve as co-chairs of the council, which is comprised of ministries of foreign affairs, foreign trade and communications. Cabinet appointments were carefully distributed among the three national communities.

Under the Dayton peace treaty's constitution, most practical powers have been awarded to the two entities, the Serb republic and the Moslem-Croat federation which control roughly half the country respectively.
